layer: markers, routes, the quest journey and the ruler (records 35, 37, 52, 46)
summary: MARKERS (48): 33 agree with the annals and gazetteer (hot springs, holy well, both bridges, all seven inns and their dishes, the five lighthouses, both battlefields with their canon dates, the Hollow Man, both sacred woods, the three pirate waters, the Sea-Watcher, the library, both circus pitches, the Còmhrag, the fair, Cidhe Beag, the panthers, the necropolis). 10 conflict and are brought to the history on the map: the silver-town note (wrong population), both Toll-dubh notes (called 'undiscovered', but found and walled in the Age of Sundering), the three standing stones (said to be unreadable, but carrying Dia-thìris words beside the unread script), the three ruins ('untold riches' the annals disprove), and the party marker (stood at Cnoc ghlas, which the journey never reaches; moved to the journey's end at Inis thais). 5 were missing from the history: the five 'random encounter' markers, which become named meeting-places with an annals event each (I, III, IV x3) and gazetteer lines. Two gazetteer entries contradicted the annals about Toll-dubh and one about Drochaid Ros fhionn; fixed. ROUTES (446: 346 trails, 174 named; 100 sea routes, 62 named; no roads at all): the history has made and crown-kept roads from the Holy Age on, so 16 routes that carry the history's roads exactly are renamed and regrouped as roads (Rathad na Mèinne, the mine road, 8 routes; Rathad na Banrighinn, 5; Rathad na Fèille, 2; An Rathad Tuath, 1). The main named routes of the map now have a making in the annals: the crown's roads of 900 (III-0145 now names An Rathad Tuath, Slighe Muileann dhearg and Slighe Baile òg), Slighe Cnoc leathan (II-0207), Ceum Ros àrsaidh (IV-0364), Rathad na Mèinne metalled (IV-0088a), the coal line laid (IV-0236a, missing from the annals though age V repairs it) and its western branch (V-0058a); and the six great sea-lanes: Slighe-mhara àrsaidh (I-0064a), Seòlaid Ros fhionn (III-0168a), Slighe-mhara Caol fhiadhaich (III-0189a, and the coal ships on it IV-0090a), Slighe-uisce reòta (III-0215), Seòlaid Ceann òg (IV-0076a; named for a quay founded 1782-1800, so dated after it), Slighe-mhara chritheanach (gazetteer). The ~200 short local tracks and lanes named for their towns are left as the island's carriers' tracks, not listed. JOURNEY (record 52): Buidheann an t-Seabhaig Luaidhe was not in the history. It becomes the council's envoys to the Hawk coast in January 1929, between the shelling of Seann Toll and the opening of the hawk-shrines (IV-0342a..e): gathered at An Cupa Dàna, Cuan dhearg (stay 9 h); on foot to Inis mhin by Seann Toll, Baile thais, Achadh dhomhain, Cnoc bheag, Ros gheal and Seann Skell (80 mi, 3+ days); rumours at Inis mhin (12 h); carriage off the roads to the grasslands above Tobar dhomhain (2 days); watch (11 h); carriage off the roads to Inis thais (2 days): nine days, with a book passage in age IV. RULER (record 46): runs from the western lane's farthest reach to the eastern lane's; it becomes James Fenn's line of 1786 (IV-0027a), 221 miles. The map's distance scale (4 mi per unit, an island 3,500 miles wide) contradicts every distance in the history; 0.2 mi per unit is proposed, and the journey and ruler figures use it.

map_edits.why: At 4 miles to the map unit Dia-thìr would be some 3,500 miles across, which no line of the history allows: Cathair dhomhain and the capital are 'a few miles apart' (II-0138, 36 units), Muileann ghlas is 'within a day's walk' of Cathair dhearg (VI-0113, 109 units), and the northern wool goes to Muileann òg 'a week on the road' by cart (V-0147, about 330 units). 0.2 miles to the unit fits all three (7 mi, 22 mi, 66 mi) and makes the island about 175 miles from west to east. It also makes the quest journey (record 52) take nine days instead of five months, and the ruler (record 46) read 221 miles. Azgaar redraws the scale bar from this value on load; the saved scale-bar text in record 5 may show the old figure until then.

map_edits.old: Muileann chiar is a mining town of 11461 people just nearby the silver mine.
map_edits.value: Muileann chiar, the silver town, stands beside the only silver seam on Dia-thìr, found in the Holy Age near the great vein and never part of it. The town's silver guild has held the seam ever since: against the Company in the Age of Strangers, and under the kingdom's charter now.
map_edits.why: The generated note gives the town 11,461 people; the burg (419) has 1,771 on the map and the gazetteer calls it 'smaller now than in its great years'. The new note says what the annals say of the seam (II-0015, IV-0101..0103, IV-0143, V-0137).

map_edits.old: Undiscovered dungeon. See One page dungeon
map_edits.value: Toll-dubh, the western shaft of the Old Ones: cut straight down through the rock, its walls tooled smooth as far as a lamp can show, with no spoil heap beside it. Quarrymen from north of the capital broke into it in the Age of Sundering and found a stair cut in the rock going down beyond their lamps. The custodians walled the entrance up, and it has not been opened since.
map_edits.why: The note was a link to a random dungeon generator calling the place 'undiscovered'. The annals have this shaft cut in the Ancient Age (I-0037), broken into and walled up (III-0149); the book says the same (age_III).

map_edits.old: Undiscovered dungeon. See One page dungeon
map_edits.value: Toll-dubh, the eastern shaft of the Old Ones, twin of the western one across the island. In the Age of Ailean a youth was let down into it on a rope of plaited hide and drawn up alive, and he never said what he had seen. Charcoal-burners found it again in the Age of Sundering, with the same cut stair as the western shaft, and the custodians walled it up. The people of Muileann ruadh keep away from it.
map_edits.why: Same as marker 19: the annals have this shaft (I-0036, I-0120) found again and walled (III-0199); it is not 'undiscovered'.

map_edits.old: Ruins of an ancient outpost. Untold riches may lie within.
map_edits.value: Ruins of a walled outpost of the Old Ones on a spur above Cathair mhòr. Its stones are dressed on the outer face only, and its single gate faces inland and was blocked with rubble from the inside. No one knows who built it.
map_edits.why: Generated 'untold riches may lie within'; the annals give the outpost's building, its walled-up gate and its abandonment (I-0032, I-0058, I-0059) and no treasure.

map_edits.old: Ruins of an ancient fortress. Untold riches may lie within.
map_edits.value: Ruins of a fortress of the Old Ones: three rings of wall and a cistern cut into the bedrock, with room for four hundred people and their beasts. It was long said to hold riches. The men of Baile ghorm who dug for them in the Holy Age found only ash, and the library's diggers found walls older than any Dia-thìrich building and no writing.
map_edits.why: The 'untold riches' of the generated note are the rumour the annals record and disprove (II-0168, V-0120).

map_edits.old: Ruins of an ancient temple. Untold riches may lie within.
map_edits.value: Ruins of a temple older than any faith on the island: a stepped platform of fitted stone whose altar is set square to the central mountains, not to the sea. Its top stone was prised off in the Ancient Age and has never been found. Edwin Lowe dug here for a season in the Age of Strangers and found cut stone, burnt bone and marks he could not read; the library has measured it and, at the asking of the district, left it undug.
map_edits.why: Replaces 'untold riches may lie within' with what the annals say (I-0035, I-0062, I-0063, IV-0140, V-0121).

event.title: The ancient sea-way
event.body: The boats of the Seann-Dhaoine keep a lane along the south-east coast, from the river mouth below Seann Dunn round the cape where Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg now stands to the bay of Ceann chaol. Flat landing-stones lie along it a day's rowing apart, and some still show the grooves of hauled keels. The Dia-thìrich call it Slighe-mhara àrsaidh, the ancient sea-way, and the fishers of that coast keep to it still.

event.title: The meeting of the cups
event.body: The keeper's cup and its three copies are carried to a spring on the moor between Àth gharbh and Tobar dhìreach, set side by side on a flat stone and filled from the spring in turn. The place is called Coinneachadh nan Cupan, the meeting of the cups, and the hill settlements come back to it whenever a cup is broken and a new one must be checked.

event.title: The stone on the neck
event.body: Caol gharbh and Caol chrom, the two harbours of the strait, send their headmen to a stone on the neck of land between them and settle the dues the salt-boats pay to each. They meet at the same stone over every quarrel about the strait after, and it is called Coinneachadh na h-Amhaich, the meeting of the neck.

event.title: Seòlaid Ros fhionn
event.body: With the salt of Ros fhionn going by sea, its boats run down the river past Caol gharbh, round the north-east cape, south along the eastern shore past Seann Tarr and Àth bheag, and back west into the bay below Caol shean, where the salt goes inland. The lane is called Seòlaid Ros fhionn after the town whose salt made it, and the eastern boats keep it long after the salt-pans fail.

event.title: The southern lane
event.body: The fishers of Caol fhiadhaich, on the wild strait of the west coast, take their boats round into the southern sea and along the whole south coast to the mouth of the Abhainn uaine, and up it to the quays of Baile thais, where they sell dried fish for grain. The older harbours of the south coast, which had not sailed beyond their own capes, begin to follow them. The lane is named for its first sailors: Slighe-mhara Caol fhiadhaich.

event.title: The ships met off the north-west
event.body: Two fishing boats out of Achadh àrsaidh, working the water off the north-west cape where the Sea-Watcher is seen, meet three ships out of the west and hail them. Neither side understands the other. The fishers turn south and the ships follow them down the coast toward Cuan shean. The fishers call the place of the meeting Coinneachadh nan Long, the meeting of the ships, and the boats of Achadh àrsaidh still slow there.

event.title: Fenn's line
event.body: On the same survey James Fenn runs a line of sights across the whole island, from the open sea off the north-west, where ships from the west first raise the land, to the water off the eastern cape. He measures it at two hundred and twenty-one miles, some forty-five of them sea at the western end. It is the first measure of Dia-thìr from side to side, and every chart the Company draws afterwards is scaled to it.

event.title: Seòlaid Ceann òg
event.body: The traders' boats from the new quay at Ceann òg go down the Abhainn ìseal past Cnoc bheag and Inis bhàn to the north coast, west along it, round the western capes, and south past Inis thais into the capital's water. Their lane is called Seòlaid Ceann òg after the quay. Off the north-west it swings far out into open sea, and there the ships bound for an Tìr Thall leave it and the ships from the west come in.

event.title: Rathad na Mèinne
event.body: The Company's road-gangs finish metalling the carriers' road from Cathair dhearg by Doire chaol and the ford of Àth chiar to the workings at Achadh dhomhain, wide enough for coal-carts to pass both ways. The carters call it Rathad na Mèinne, the mine road. The posts with the crown's sign that had marked it since the Age of Sundering are left standing along it.

event.title: The coal ships' lane
event.body: From the landing at Seann Toll the coal barges go down the Abhainn uaine to Ceann leathan, where the Company's ships load at the river mouth and go out by the southern lane, Slighe-mhara Caol fhiadhaich, west along the south coast to the wild strait and the open sea. The fishers of the south coast, who had used the lane for five hundred years, learn to keep out of the coal ships' way.

event.title: The coal line laid
event.body: The Company lays an iron railway from the yards at Muileann chrom down to Cathair dhearg and the quays of Ros dhomhain, its engines burning coal. The carters' guild of Doire chaol, which had hauled the coal on Rathad na Mèinne for eighty years, loses the long haul within a year. The railway is called the coal line from the first.

event.title: The meeting on the moor road
event.body: The people turned out of the closed district send their eldest to the custodians of Muileann dhomhain, who meet them at a standing stone on the moor road below the town rather than let the Company's clerks see them in the town hall. At the stone the custodians lend them the land at the edge of the fenced ground. The place is called Coinneachadh an Fhearainn, the meeting of the land.

event.title: The crews meet on the moor
event.body: Crew-leaders from Baile gharbh and the other northern pits meet at night on the moor above Cnoc naomh and fix the week of their rising. Each brings a stone of spoil from his own pit, and the stones are left in a cairn. The place is called Coinneachadh a' Mhonaidh, the meeting of the moor.

event.title: The Leaden Hawk company
event.body: At An Cupa Dàna, the inn at Cuan dhearg, seven hawk-faithful crewmen of the river towns wait nine hours for the council's letters to the Hawk coast, and leave with them at dark. Each wears a hawk cast in lead from the cartridges taken at the store at Muileann chrom, and the record calls them Buidheann an t-Seabhaig Luaidhe, the Leaden Hawk company.

event.title: The Leaden Hawk walks to the Hawk coast
event.body: The company goes on foot and lightly laden: past the burned stage at Seann Toll, through Baile thais, up over the hills by Achadh dhomhain and Cuan bheag, down the Abhainn ìseal by Ceann òg and Inis ìseal to Cnoc bheag, and along the Hawk coast by Inis bhàn, Ros gheal and Seann Skell to Inis mhin, some eighty miles in a little over three days. At every hawk-house on the way they read the council's letter aloud, and at Seann Skell they leave it with Ìomhar Seabhag.

event.title: Rumours at Inis mhin
event.body: At Inis mhin, the northern landing the humans had walled, the company lies twelve hours in a boat-shed and hears that Strake's constables ride the western roads out of Ros bheag every day. They hire a carriage from a carter of the town and leave the roads altogether.

event.title: The watch in the grasslands
event.body: Two days by carriage across country, off every road, bring the company to the grasslands above Tobar dhomhain in the western hills. They lie eleven hours in the long grass over the road from Ros bheag to the concession and count the constables' riders who pass. The company's own list gives forty-one riders, and none of them going north.

event.title: The Leaden Hawk at Inis thais
event.body: Two more days by carriage, still off the roads, bring the company down to Inis thais, nine days after it left Cuan dhearg. The priests of Clach hear the council's letter in the Direwolf's temple. They will send no men, but they close the harbour of Inis thais to the Company's ships and give the hawk-faithful the use of the Wolf's roads. The Leaden Hawk ends its road there, and its seven join the hawk company when it is mustered at the western Seann Skell.

event.title: The western branch
event.body: The Rail Board carries a branch of the coal line west from Cathair dhearg to the port of Seann Bhral, with a spur north to the pits at Àth leathan, so that the western workings can send their coal east by rail.

annals_edit.old: The roads are marked with posts bearing the crown's sign.
annals_edit.new: The roads are marked with posts bearing the crown's sign: the carriers' road down to Cathair dhearg, An Rathad Tuath over the pass by Muileann fhada, Slighe Muileann dhearg south from the hills by Muileann chrom, and Slighe Baile òg down to the southern Seann Skell.
annals_edit.why: Names the crown's roads with their names on the map (routes 16/111.., 3, 17, 98), so the main named roads have a making in the history.

annals_edit.old: Queen Catrìona has the road from the capital south by Am Buabhall Fortanach laid with stone,
annals_edit.new: Queen Catrìona has the road from the capital south by Baile shean and Am Buabhall Fortanach at Doire shean laid with stone,
annals_edit.why: Inis thais lies west of the capital and Am Buabhall Fortanach south of Inis thais, so the road 'south by' the inn only makes sense by the way the map's routes run (Baile shean, Doire shean, then north to Inis thais); the route is now named Rathad na Banrighinn on the map.

annals_edit.old: The coasting grain barges of Inis mhòr are laid up for good as the roads improve.
annals_edit.new: The coasting grain barges of Inis mhòr, which had sailed Slighe-uisce reòta, the frozen way along the north coast from Ros chiar to Caol mhin, since the Holy Age, are laid up for good as the roads improve.
annals_edit.why: Gives the northern sea route Slighe-uisce reòta (route 383, Ros chiar to Caol mhin) its place in the history.

annals_edit.old: The road from Cathair dhearg to Muileann òg is widened and metalled for the fair's carts, passing Dùn chrom, which takes a toll at its gate and grows on it.
annals_edit.new: The road from Cathair dhearg to Muileann òg is widened and metalled for the fair's carts, passing Dùn chrom, which takes a toll at its gate and grows on it. As far as Muileann ghlas it runs on the old coal road; the new stretches are called Rathad na Fèille.
annals_edit.why: Names the fair road as the map now does (routes 71, 50).

annals_edit.old: for the upkeep of the road to Cnoc leathan.
annals_edit.new: for the upkeep of the road to Cnoc leathan, Slighe Cnoc leathan.
annals_edit.why: Gives the long south-eastern route Slighe Cnoc leathan (route 264) its making in the history.

annals_edit.new: to hold the coast road, Ceum Ros àrsaidh.
annals_edit.why: The coast road north of Ros bheag is the map's Ceum Ros àrsaidh (route 301, Ros àrsaidh to Baile dhìreach).

annals_edit.old: Baile thais, where the coal road from the central mountains meets the east coast,
annals_edit.new: Baile thais, where the coal road from the central mountains comes down to the Abhainn uaine above the gulf,
annals_edit.why: Baile thais is not on the east coast: it lies in the middle of the island where the Abhainn uaine reaches the gulf (gazetteer 44; map 853,340).

gazetteer_edit.old: The hollow called Toll-dubh lies in the hills behind it; it has never been mapped, and the town's people do not go near it.
gazetteer_edit.new: The shaft called Toll-dubh lies in the hills behind it. Quarrymen broke into it in the Age of Sundering and found a stair cut in the rock going down beyond their lamps, and the custodians walled it up; the town's people do not go near it.

gazetteer_edit.old: The unexplored hollow called Toll-dubh lies close by, and the townsfolk keep away from it.
gazetteer_edit.new: The eastern Toll-dubh, the shaft of the Old Ones that charcoal-burners found again in the Age of Sundering and the custodians walled up, lies close by, and the townsfolk keep away from it.

gazetteer_edit.old: Drochaid Ros fhionn, the old crossing, is still standing but has seen little traffic since the local trade dried up.
gazetteer_edit.new: Drochaid Ros fhionn, the old crossing, is still standing. It has seen little traffic since the salt went by sea, except for the century when the Company's coal carts crossed it on the eastern coal road, and it fell silent again when the eastern pits flooded in the Severance war. The salt-boats' lane round the east cape, Seòlaid Ros fhionn, is named for the town.
Its inn, An Cupa Dàna, is where Buidheann an t-Seabhaig Luaidhe, the Leaden Hawk company, gathered in the first winter of the Severance war before walking to the Hawk coast.
In the first winter of the Severance war the Leaden Hawk company, Buidheann an t-Seabhaig Luaidhe, lay twelve hours in the town and heard of the constables riding the western roads.
The grassland above the village is where the Leaden Hawk company kept its watch on the road from Ros bheag in the first winter of the Severance war.

Buidheann an t-Seabhaig Luaidhe, the Leaden Hawk company sent by the council in the Severance war, ended its road at the temple here; the priests of Clach kept the city out of the war but shut its harbour to the Company's ships.
On the moor above the town is Coinneachadh a' Mhonaidh, the cairn where the crew-leaders of the northern pits fixed the week of their rising.
The village stands on land the custodians of Muileann dhomhain lent to the people of the closed district at Coinneachadh an Fhearainn, the standing stone on the moor road.
Its headmen and Caol chrom's meet at Coinneachadh na h-Amhaich, the stone on the neck of land between the two harbours, to settle the dues of the strait.
Its headmen and Caol gharbh's meet at Coinneachadh na h-Amhaich, the stone on the neck of land between the two harbours, to settle the dues of the strait.
Its boats first met the humans' ships at sea, off the north-west cape at the place they call Coinneachadh nan Long.
Coinneachadh nan Cupan, the spring where the keeper's stone cup was first checked against its copies, lies on the moor between the ford and Tobar dhìreach.
The ford carries Rathad na Mèinne, the mine road from the capital to the hills.
Rathad na Banrighinn, Queen Catrìona's stone road from the capital to Inis thais, runs through the village past the tavern.
Rathad na Fèille, the fair road, was metalled from Cathair dhearg in the fair's first years.
Slighe-mhara Caol fhiadhaich, the southern sea-lane, comes up the river to its quays.
The southern sea-lane, Slighe-mhara Caol fhiadhaich, is named for its fishers, who first sailed it round the south coast in the long quiet centuries.
Seòlaid Ceann òg, the western lane round the capes to the capital's water, is named for its quay.
Slighe-mhara àrsaidh, the ancient sea-way of the Old Ones, begins at the river mouth below the town and runs round the south-east cape to Ceann chaol.
Slighe-uisce reòta, the frozen way along the north coast to Caol mhin, begins at its harbour; the grain barges of Inis mhòr sailed it until the roads took their trade.
Pilgrims' boats from the southern Seann Skell come round to its landing by Slighe-mhara chritheanach, the shaking sea-way, named for the swell off the south cape.
Slighe Ceann mhin, the long road down the east of the island to Seann Dunn, begins at its gate.
The coast road north from Ros bheag, Ceum Ros àrsaidh, starts below its walls; Strake's constables held it in the last months of the Severance war.
Slighe Cnoc leathan, the road south past An Taigh-òsta Grianach, has been kept up by the inn's own toll since Anna Ruadh's charter.
The coal line, the railway the Company laid to Cathair dhearg, was built from its yards.

text_edit.old: Where the strangers were in the days between, the rolls do not say.
text_edit.new: Where the strangers were in the days between, the rolls do not say. The fishers of Achadh àrsaidh say it for them: their boats met the three ships off the north-west cape and led them down the coast ({{date:IV-0001a}}), and they still call the place Coinneachadh nan Long.
text_edit.why: Book line for the new encounter marker 45 (IV-0001a).

text_edit.old: At Seann Skell Ìomhar Seabhag declared that the war was Mòd's own hunger turned back on those who had fed it, and the hawk-shrines of the west became recruiting-houses.
text_edit.new: Earlier that winter the council had sent its letters to the Hawk coast by the hands of seven hawk-faithful crewmen of the river towns, who wore hawks cast from the lead of the cartridges taken at Muileann chrom and were called Buidheann an t-Seabhaig Luaidhe, the Leaden Hawk company. They gathered at An Cupa Dàna in Cuan dhearg ({{date:IV-0342a}}) and walked north past the burned stage at Seann Toll, over the hills by Achadh dhomhain and down the Abhainn ìseal to Cnoc bheag, reading the letter at every hawk-house along the coast to Inis mhin. There they heard that Strake's constables rode the western roads, and they went on by carriage across country, off every road, watched the Ros bheag road a night and a day from the grasslands above Tobar dhomhain ({{date:IV-0342d}}), and came down to Inis thais nine days after they had set out. The priests of Clach would send no men, but they shut the harbour of Inis thais to the Company's ships ({{date:IV-0342e}}). At Seann Skell Ìomhar Seabhag declared that the war was Mòd's own hunger turned back on those who had fed it, and the hawk-shrines of the west became recruiting-houses.
text_edit.why: The quest journey (record 52) as a passage of the Age of Strangers book, before the hawk-shrines open (IV-0348).

unsure: Record 1 distance scale 4 -> 0.2 mi per map unit is a global change: it alters every length and area Azgaar reports (no square-mile or mile figure from the map appears in the history today). If it is refused, the journey times stated in IV-0342a..e and the book (three days on foot, two and two by carriage, nine in all) and Fenn's 221 miles no longer match the map, which would give 64 days on foot, 36 and 46 by carriage and 4,431 miles.

Route 119 (Ceum Àth shean, 212 units) carries a 24-32 unit stretch of both Rathad na Mèinne and Rathad na Banrighinn just south of the capital (between Baile ìseal and Cill thais/Baile chiar); left as a trail, the two roads show a short gap there unless 119 is split at cell of Baile ìseal (burg 320). Route 233 likewise carries 15 units of the queen's road between Àth fhiadhaich and Baile Mòr fhionn.

Regrouping routes to 'roads' needs the SVG (record 5) path elements moved from <g id='trails'> into <g id='roads'> (currently an empty self-closing element); burg_features.py's extend_routes shows the byte-safe way the pipeline edits route paths.

The coal line (railway) cannot be drawn: Azgaar has no railway route group. If wanted, a custom route group 'railways' could carry Muileann chrom - Cathair dhearg, the Sloc Mòr extension, Ceann leathan and the western branch.

The five encounter markers are reinterpreted as meeting-places; their events are new history (the meeting of the cups, the stone on the neck, the ships met off the north-west, the meeting on the moor road, the crews on the moor). IV-0001a adds an answer to the book's 'where the strangers were in the days between, the rolls do not say' as the fishers' telling, not the rolls'.

Standing stones: the history already holds both that Calbh Cnoc ghorm 'carries the doctrine itself, complete' (I-0073, canon) and that Holy Age scholars could not read it (II-0167). The canon events are left as they are; the map note phrases the doctrine as what the people of Cnoc ghorm say it carries.
V-0054 (Baile thais 'meets the east coast') may also be touched by the ports/rivers layer.
Suffixed ids (I-0064a, IV-0090a, ...) were free when written; other layers adding events after the same ids may collide.
Inn marker notes name drinks the history never mentions (shiny water, hot juice, green brandy, black water); these are left as agreeing detail, not added to the annals.
